questions.prompt: What should primarily drive your choice of Redis data structure?

options.text: Always use Strings for simplicity
The access pattern — whether you need order, uniqueness, ranking, object fields, or a durable log
The alphabetical order of command names
Whichever type uses the most memory

questions.explanation: Good modeling matches the problem's access pattern to the structure that supports it directly (Set for uniqueness, Sorted Set for ranking, Stream for a durable log, and so on).

questions.prompt: In core Redis, how do you look data up by something other than its primary key?

options.text: You can't — Redis only supports key lookups, ever
Build a secondary index yourself (e.g. a Set/Sorted Set of IDs) or use the Query Engine to index content
Run KEYS on every request
Store everything in one giant hash

questions.explanation: Core Redis looks up by key, so you maintain your own index structures (like a Set of IDs) for non-key lookups — or use the Query Engine to index hashes/JSON automatically.

questions.prompt: Which are Redis modeling anti-patterns? Select all that apply.

options.text: Big keys — a single collection with millions of elements
Unbounded collections that only ever grow
Using KEYS in production to find keys
Giving cache keys a TTL

questions.explanation: Big keys, unbounded growth, and KEYS in production are anti-patterns. Giving cache keys a TTL is a good practice, not an anti-pattern.

questions.prompt: Which structures best fit a leaderboard and a reliable, replayable job queue, respectively?

options.text: A List and a Set
A Sorted Set and a Stream (with consumer groups)
A String and a Hash
A HyperLogLog and a Bitmap

questions.explanation: A Sorted Set keeps players ranked by score; a Stream with consumer groups gives at-least-once, replayable, multi-worker job processing.

questions.prompt: A fixed-window rate limiter increments a per-window counter and sets an ______ on it so the window resets automatically. (one word — the key-lifetime concept)
questions.explanation: INCR the counter and set an EXPIRE (a TTL) matching the window; when it expires the limit resets to zero with no scheduled job.

questions.prompt: When is Redis the WRONG primary tool?

options.text: When you need a fast cache in front of a database
When you need rich ad-hoc queries/joins, data much larger than RAM, or strong transactional guarantees with rollback
When you need a leaderboard
When you need a session store

questions.explanation: Redis is a poor fit for query-heavy reporting, datasets far larger than RAM, or strict transactional/rollback needs — use a purpose-built database (often with Redis as a cache in front).
